# Ledger scale bench

Generated by `scripts/bench-ledger.ts` (`npx tsx scripts/bench-ledger.ts --sizes 10000,100000 --md
docs/evidence/ledger-scale.md`), Node v22.23.3, on the dev host (not the Node 22 clean-room container this
round — a plain local run; `node:sqlite` confirmed real via the bench's own `node=` line either way). **Sizes
are 10,000 and 100,000 runs only, both real, both measured — 1,000,000 is a labelled extrapolation only (see
below), never claimed as measured.** This machine was running other parallel work at the same time (see
"What's noisy this round" below) — `rebuild`/`catchup*`/point-op numbers are trustworthy; `placeBroad`/
`placeNarrow` are not, this round.

## Bottom line: plan 2c Phase C, "before C3" — the catch-up O(n)

`lab/research/2026-09-28-graph-index-scale.md` §1 measured `catchup1` growing with ledger size (91.8 ms at
10k → 431.2 ms at 100k) and flagged it as a bug to find and fix before building the graph tier on top of the
same catch-up path. **Found: it was never in `src/ledger/index.ts` — it was a bug in this bench script.**

`benchCatchUp` measured its per-sample closure through `timeCalls`, a generic helper that times its OWN
wall-clock span around calling the closure. The closure separately computed its own `ms` (wrapping only the
`nextRunNumber` call) and `return`ed it — but `timeCalls` never reads a callback's return value, it only
records how long the whole call took. So every reported `catchup1`/`catchup50` sample was actually timing:
copy the fixture's log + index.db into a fresh temp dir (fsynced) → append → fsync → the real catch-up →
`rmSync` the whole temp dir recursively. Copying and deleting O(n) bytes of fixture data (the log is
~153 MB at 100k, the index ~63-77 MB) on every single sample is exactly what made the row grow with n — the
real catch-up call buried inside it was never the thing being measured.

**Confirmed two ways:**
- A throwaway trace build (`process.hrtime.bigint()` markers dropped into `tryOpenAndCheck`/`catchUpInPlace`/
  `runSqlite`, then reverted — never committed) run against this same bench showed the real per-call cost
  (open + the two freshness checks + the actual scan/insert/commit + close) at n=100,000 is **~14-40 ms**, not
  the ~430-650 ms the buggy harness was reporting for the identical calls in the identical run. The commit
  step itself (WAL fsync) does grow mildly with total db size (~5 ms at 10k → ~20 ms at 100k) but that's a
  small, roughly-constant SQLite fsync cost, not the O(n) the research note was worried about.
- Fixing only the timing (below) drops `catchup1` from 431 → 13.7 ms and `catchup50` from 497 → 38.7 ms at
  100k, with **no other line in `src/ledger/index.ts` touched** — if there had been a real O(n) in the
  production catch-up path, a bench-timing fix alone could not have changed its cost.

**Conclusion: this is a bench-fixture-only artifact, not a production bug.** `src/ledger/index.ts`'s catch-up
path (`tryOpenAndCheck`, `catchUpInPlace`, `hashLogRange`) was not touched — its own fingerprint check already
only hashes the last complete line (`fpStart`→`upto`), not the whole log, so there was no O(n) hiding there to
begin with. **Fix applied only to `scripts/bench-ledger.ts`**: `benchCatchUp` now measures `nextRunNumber`
directly into its own `durations` array instead of routing through `timeCalls`'s generic (and here,
misleading) wrapper. Every other row still uses `timeCalls` correctly — for those ops the timed closure really
is just the operation under test, with no extra per-sample setup inside it.

Two more (unrelated but pre-existing) bugs in this same bench script surfaced once the run was actually
inspected closely, and are fixed in the same commit as the timing fix since they live in the same file and
were making the `class` row silently measure the wrong thing:
- **`benchClassCall`'s request used the pre-2b flat `ask.reach` shape** (10 questions, no concerns/decisions
  split) — the current contract's schema rejects that outright (`exit: 2`, a validation stop), so this row was
  quietly timing a ~10 ms validation failure, never a real paid call, and reporting `calls: -1`. Rewritten to
  the current schema's `concerns:` (3 categories x 3 probes, `quick` depth's exact 3k x 3 shape) plus a
  `decisions:` block (2 categories, the minimum).
- **Once the request validated, it immediately hit the default budget cap** (`src/config/defaults.ts`:
  $5 / 500 runs, `per: total`, counted across the WHOLE ledger) — the synthetic ledger's own cost
  (`costUsd: 0.01` x n) is $100 at 10k and $1,000 at 100k, so the paid call stopped with `exit: 3` (budget cap
  reached) before it could append anything. Fixed by writing a generous project-local `config.yaml` (budget
  scaled to n) into the bench's own temp project before the call — `DEFAULT_CONFIG` itself is untouched. Both
  sizes now show `exit: 0, calls: 1` — a genuine paid call, same as the row is meant to demonstrate.

## What's noisy this round (not chased further)

`placeBroad`/`placeNarrow` at 100k show ~6.5-6.9 s this round, versus ~360/84 ms in the last committed run.
`view.ts` (what these two rows exercise) was not touched by anyone this round, and this bench run happened
back-to-back with several other 100k-record benches on the same shared, non-containerized dev machine while
other parallel work was also running — the doc's own prior note already flags this op as noisy on a loaded
box ("the 100k p95 (8.4 s on one of 8 samples) is a real outlier ... not chased further"). This round's p50
being high too, not just p95, points at sustained machine load rather than a code regression, but it wasn't
re-verified on a quiet box or in the clean-room container — flagged here rather than asserted either way.
Not this task's target (the O(n) catch-up investigation above was); leaving it for a future round to
re-measure in the container, the way the original baseline was.

## 1,000,000: extrapolated, not measured

Not run this round either — out of scope (10k and 100k only), and Task 27's own finding still applies:
`toJsonl`-shaped generation runs into Node's `buffer.constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH` (≈512 MiB) somewhere north
of ~500,000 records on this build. With the O(n) catch-up finding above resolved (it was never real), a 1M
ledger's catch-up cost is expected to stay flat, the same way 10k→100k stayed flat here; `rebuild`'s own cost,
not tuned this round, would still scale with the untouched db/log ratio and rebuild path.

## Rebuild / maintenance cadence

Unchanged from prior rounds' own finding: no proactive, size-triggered rebuild is needed — a SQL table's rows
grow proportionally with the ledger, and a catch-up only ever touches the bytes actually added since the
last one (now genuinely confirmed flat with n, not just assumed). The self-heal triggers (missing, unreadable,
a suspicious size that fails quick_check, a schema-version mismatch, a log shorter than `upto`, or a
fingerprint mismatch) are unchanged by this round — only this bench's own measurement of catch-up (and the
`class` row's request shape and budget headroom) changed.
